papers.title: Attention in Motion: Using Scroll Tracking to Measure the Dynamics of Preferential Choice
papers.abstract: Management Science, Ahead of Print.
papers.rq: Can scroll-tracking data capture the dynamics of attention and preferential choice during online decision-making?
papers.method: Scroll-tracking methodology applied to online choice tasks, measuring how consumers allocate visual attention across options over time as a behavioral proxy for preference formation
papers.keyFinding: Scroll behavior reveals systematic patterns in how attention evolves during choice, with deeper and repeated scrolling to an option predicting selection; the dynamics of scrolling provide richer information about preference strength and decision process than final choices alone
papers.whyItMatters: Offers researchers and firms a low-cost, scalable tool to measure attention and preference formation in natural online environments without eye-tracking equipment, enabling better understanding of how digital interface design influences consumer decisions

papers.title: Can Stablecoins Be Stable?
papers.abstract: Management Science, Ahead of Print.
papers.rq: Can algorithmic and collateralized stablecoins maintain price stability, and what mechanisms drive or undermine their pegs?
papers.method: Theoretical modeling combined with empirical analysis of on-chain transaction data and price dynamics across major stablecoin protocols
papers.keyFinding: Stablecoins face fundamental stability challenges; algorithmic stablecoins are prone to death spirals under adverse conditions while collateralized stablecoins are more robust but still vulnerable to collateral shocks and bank-run dynamics
papers.whyItMatters: Stablecoins are critical infrastructure for crypto markets and potentially broader payments systems; understanding their failure modes is essential for risk management and regulatory design

papers.title: Competition versus coordination: The impact of flattening government on firm creation and aggregate productivity
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Lingran Yuan, Qizheng Zhang, Binlei Gong
papers.rq: Does flattening government hierarchies (reducing administrative layers) boost firm creation and aggregate productivity by increasing inter-jurisdictional competition or improving coordination?
papers.method: Exploits China's county-direct administration reforms as a quasi-natural experiment, using difference-in-differences estimation on panel data covering Chinese firms and regional economic outcomes across provinces that adopted the reform at different times.
papers.keyFinding: Flattening government structures increases firm creation and aggregate productivity, primarily through intensifying competition among local governments rather than through improved administrative coordination, as jurisdictions gain more direct fiscal and regulatory autonomy.
papers.whyItMatters: Provides causal evidence that streamlining bureaucratic hierarchies can stimulate entrepreneurship and economic dynamism in developing economies, with implications for administrative reform policy in China and other centralized states seeking to improve allocative efficiency.

papers.title: Cyclical behavior in large location games
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Gary Charness, Daniel Friedman, Weinan Gong, Lones Smith
papers.rq: Do players in large location games exhibit cyclical strategic behavior rather than converging to Nash equilibrium?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment with large-group location games where participants choose positions on a line or circle, analyzed for dynamic patterns in repeated play
papers.keyFinding: Players systematically cycle through strategies rather than settling at Nash equilibrium predictions, with aggregate behavior showing persistent oscillatory dynamics driven by best-response chasing
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the standard equilibrium convergence assumption in spatial competition models relevant to political positioning, product differentiation, and market entry decisions

papers.title: Democracy and pro-market sentiments
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Veeshan Rayamajhee
papers.rq: Does democratic governance causally increase pro-market sentiments among citizens?
papers.method: Cross-country empirical analysis using survey data on economic attitudes, exploiting variation in democratic institutions with instrumental variable and fixed-effects approaches
papers.keyFinding: Democracy significantly boosts pro-market sentiments, suggesting that political freedom and economic liberalism are complementary rather than in tension
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding whether democracy cultivates market-friendly attitudes has implications for reform sequencing in developing economies and the political sustainability of economic liberalization

papers.title: Diagnostic uncertainty and insurance coverage in credence goods markets: An experiment
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Loukas Balafoutas, Helena Fornwagner, Rudolf Kerschbamer, Matthias Sutter, Marina Tverdostup
papers.rq: How does diagnostic uncertainty and insurance coverage affect fraud and efficiency in credence goods markets?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment simulating a credence goods market (e.g., medical or repair services) where experts diagnose and treat consumers under varying conditions of diagnostic uncertainty and insurance coverage
papers.keyFinding: Diagnostic uncertainty increases inefficiency and fraud in credence goods markets, while insurance coverage amplifies these problems by reducing consumer price sensitivity and increasing expert incentives to over-treat or misreport
papers.whyItMatters: Credence goods markets like healthcare and auto repair are pervasive; understanding how uncertainty and insurance jointly distort expert behavior has direct implications for market regulation, insurance design, and consumer protection policy

papers.title: Effect of social information on competition choice
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Ritwik Banerjee, Lata Gangadharan, Anand Kumar, Srinivasan Murali
papers.rq: Does social information about others' competition choices influence an individual's decision to enter competitive versus non-competitive payment schemes?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment in which participants chose between a piece-rate and a tournament payment scheme after receiving information about the choices made by others in their reference group
papers.keyFinding: Social information significantly affects competition entry decisions, with individuals conforming to the observed choices of peers, suggesting that competition choice is shaped by social influence rather than purely individual ability assessments
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding how peer information drives tournament entry has implications for designing incentive structures in workplaces and educational settings, and helps explain gender gaps or under-representation in competitive environments if social norms discourage certain groups from competing

papers.title: Experimental methods: Revisiting the commandments of experimental economics
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Uri Gneezy
papers.rq: Should the classic commandments of experimental economics be revised in light of modern behavioral and field experiment practices?
papers.method: Conceptual and methodological review drawing on decades of experimental economics literature and the author's own research experience
papers.keyFinding: Gneezy revisits the foundational rules of experimental economics—such as no deception, salient monetary incentives, and induced value theory—and argues that several commandments need updating or relaxing to accommodate the realities of modern experimental practice, particularly in behavioral and field settings
papers.whyItMatters: Experimental economics is at a methodological crossroads as it increasingly intersects with psychology and field work; clarifying which rules are essential versus outdated helps researchers design better experiments and improves credibility of findings across disciplines

papers.title: Fair inequality? Lab evidence from Kenya
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Kjetil Bjorvatn, Nicola D. Coniglio, Arne Nasgowitz
papers.rq: Do Kenyan participants consider certain forms of inequality fair, and how do fairness perceptions shape tolerance for inequality in a lab setting?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment conducted in Kenya using incentivized games to elicit preferences over inequality, likely involving distributional choice tasks and survey measures of fairness attitudes
papers.keyFinding: Participants distinguish between fair and unfair inequality, showing greater tolerance for inequality perceived as earned or merit-based compared to arbitrary inequality, suggesting fairness norms mediate inequality acceptance
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding when people accept versus reject inequality is critical for predicting redistributive preferences and designing effective social policy, particularly in high-inequality developing economies like Kenya

papers.title: Inflation targeting and income inequality
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Hippolyte Balima, Alexandru Minea, Cezara Vinturis
papers.rq: Does the adoption of inflation targeting monetary policy regimes affect income inequality?
papers.method: Empirical cross-country analysis using a difference-in-differences or treatment effects approach comparing countries that adopted inflation targeting versus those that did not, likely using panel data
papers.keyFinding: Inflation targeting adoption has a significant effect on income inequality, with evidence suggesting it may reduce inequality in adopting countries relative to non-adopters
papers.whyItMatters: Monetary policy frameworks are typically evaluated on macroeconomic stability grounds, but this research highlights distributional consequences of central bank regime choices, informing debates on whether inflation targeting serves broad social welfare goals

papers.title: Labor market penalty for single mothers
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Somdeep Chatterjee, Ralitza Dimova, Shubham Ojha
papers.rq: Do single mothers face a labor market penalty relative to partnered mothers or childless women, and what drives any observed gaps?
papers.method: Empirical analysis using observational labor market data, likely decomposition methods to isolate the single-mother penalty from observable and unobservable characteristics
papers.keyFinding: Single mothers experience a significant labor market penalty—in wages, employment probability, or job quality—compared to partnered mothers and childless women, with the gap only partially explained by observable differences in human capital or demographics
papers.whyItMatters: Highlights compounding disadvantages faced by single mothers who shoulder both caregiving burdens and labor market discrimination, informing targeted policy interventions around childcare, anti-discrimination, and social transfers

papers.title: Macroeconomic expectations: Formation, measurement, and consequences
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 23 May 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & OrganizationAuthor(s): Zeno Enders, Stefan T. Trautmann, Dmitri V. Vinogradov
papers.rq: How do economic agents form macroeconomic expectations, how can those expectations be measured, and what are their consequences for economic outcomes?
papers.method: Review and synthesis of theoretical and empirical literature on expectation formation, survey-based measurement approaches, and evidence on how expectations affect macroeconomic behavior
papers.keyFinding: Macroeconomic expectations deviate systematically from rational benchmark predictions; measurement tools such as surveys and experiments reveal heterogeneous, biased, and context-dependent belief formation that has meaningful downstream effects on consumption, investment, and policy transmission
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding how expectations form and how to measure them accurately is critical for monetary and fiscal policy design, since models assuming rational expectations may mispredict how households and firms respond to economic shocks or policy announcements

papers.title: Making organization’s cost salient: A natural field experiment
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Fuhai Hong, Yohanes E. Riyanto, Jubo Yan, Yuanyuan Huo

papers.title: Maternity leave and labour market outcomes
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Purna Banerjee, Shreya Biswas, Debojyoti Mazumder
papers.rq: How does maternity leave policy affect women's labor market outcomes?
papers.method: Empirical analysis using variation in maternity leave legislation, likely exploiting policy changes as a natural experiment to identify causal effects on employment, wages, and career progression
papers.keyFinding: Maternity leave entitlements have significant effects on women's labor market outcomes, with evidence suggesting trade-offs between short-term job protection and longer-term wage or employment penalties depending on leave duration and generosity
papers.whyItMatters: Informs policymakers designing parental leave systems about unintended consequences for female employment and the gender wage gap, balancing worker protection with labor market efficiency

papers.title: On the stability of social risk preferences for health and wealth
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Arthur E. Attema, Olivier L’Haridon, Gijs van de Kuilen
papers.rq: Are social risk preferences for health and wealth stable over time and across elicitation methods?
papers.method: Longitudinal experimental study eliciting social risk preferences (inequality aversion and social risk attitudes) for both health and wealth domains across multiple time points and measurement approaches
papers.keyFinding: Social risk preferences exhibit moderate to high temporal stability, though some inconsistencies emerge across elicitation methods, suggesting preferences are genuine but measurement-sensitive constructs
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding whether social risk preferences are stable informs whether they can be reliably used in cost-effectiveness analysis, healthcare resource allocation, and social welfare policy decisions

papers.title: Play to your strengths: Incumbency effect and issue emphasis in Brazilian local elections
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Leila Pereira
papers.rq: Do incumbent candidates in Brazilian local elections strategically emphasize issues where they have a performance advantage, and does this emphasis translate into electoral gains?
papers.method: Empirical analysis of Brazilian municipal election data, likely combining candidate campaign platforms or speech data with electoral outcomes and incumbency status using regression-based identification strategies
papers.keyFinding: Incumbents strategically emphasize policy issues on which they have demonstrated strong performance, and this issue emphasis generates a measurable electoral advantage over challengers
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals how incumbents exploit informational advantages through agenda-setting and issue ownership, shaping voter perceptions and undermining electoral accountability in developing-country contexts

papers.title: Pluralistic ignorance and climate policies: Information provision experiment
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Laura Galdikiene, Jurate Jaraite, Agne Kajackaite
papers.rq: Do people misperceive others' support for climate policies, and can correcting this pluralistic ignorance increase individual support for such policies?
papers.method: Information provision experiment providing participants with accurate data about peers' climate policy attitudes to correct misperceptions
papers.keyFinding: Individuals systematically underestimate public support for climate policies, and providing accurate social norm information about true peer support levels can shift individual policy preferences upward
papers.whyItMatters: Pluralistic ignorance may be a key barrier to climate action; simple, low-cost information interventions could unlock broader public and political support for climate policies by revealing latent majority backing

papers.title: Sanctions without sanctimony: Why do states impose sanctions?
papers.abstract: Publication date: August 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 248Author(s): Daniel J. D’Amico, Cameron Tilley, Joshua D. Ammons, Eric H. Wilhelm
papers.rq: Why do states choose to impose economic sanctions, and what factors drive that decision beyond stated moral or political justifications?
papers.method: Empirical analysis of state-level sanctioning behavior, likely combining quantitative cross-country data with institutional and political economy frameworks to isolate determinants of sanction imposition
papers.keyFinding: States impose sanctions driven primarily by domestic political and economic incentives rather than purely normative or humanitarian motivations, suggesting sanctimony in sanction rhetoric masks self-interested state behavior
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the true motivations behind sanctions clarifies their effectiveness and legitimacy as foreign policy tools, with implications for international relations, targeted economies, and the credibility of multilateral institutions

papers.title: Self-employment income tax evasion and inequality
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Martina Bazzoli, Paolo Di Caro, Francesco Figari, Carlo V. Fiorio, Marco Manzo
papers.rq: How does self-employment income tax evasion affect economic inequality?
papers.method: Likely combines tax administrative data with survey data and microsimulation to estimate unreported self-employment income and its distributional consequences in Italy
papers.keyFinding: Self-employment income tax evasion significantly distorts measured inequality, with evasion concentrated among self-employed individuals reducing the true progressivity of the tax system and worsening actual income inequality relative to official statistics
papers.whyItMatters: Official inequality measures may systematically understate true disparities if self-employment tax evasion is widespread; accurate measurement is critical for designing effective redistribution and tax enforcement policy

papers.title: Targeting attitudes to combat sexual harassment: A randomized intervention in the Norwegian military
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Olle Folke, Torbjørn Hanson, Åshild A. Johnsen, Andreas Kotsadam, Johanna Rickne
papers.rq: Can a randomized intervention targeting attitudes reduce sexual harassment in the Norwegian military?
papers.method: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) deployed within the Norwegian military, testing an attitude-change intervention against a control group
papers.keyFinding: The attitude-targeting intervention produced measurable reductions in sexual harassment, suggesting that shifting underlying attitudes—not just awareness or rules—is an effective lever for behavior change in institutional settings
papers.whyItMatters: Sexual harassment in military institutions is a persistent and costly problem; demonstrating that a scalable attitude-based RCT can move the needle provides a policy-relevant blueprint for other hierarchical organizations worldwide

papers.title: The impact of growth on the transmission of patience
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Domenico Delli Gatti, Jakob Grazzini, Domenico Massaro, Fabrizio Panebianco
papers.rq: How does economic growth affect the intergenerational transmission of patience (time preferences)?
papers.method: Theoretical modeling, likely combining overlapping generations framework with cultural transmission mechanisms to examine how growth dynamics shape the evolution of patience across generations.
papers.keyFinding: Economic growth influences the transmission of patience across generations, with growth conditions affecting whether patient or impatient preferences spread through a population over time, suggesting a two-way relationship between growth and time preferences.
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding how macroeconomic conditions shape the cultural transmission of preferences has implications for long-run development traps, inequality, and why some societies sustain growth while others do not — patience being a key driver of savings and investment.

papers.title: The virtues of lab experiments
papers.abstract: Publication date: July 2026Source: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 247Author(s): Gary Charness, James C. Cox, Catherine C. Eckel, Charles A. Holt, Brian Jabarian
papers.rq: What are the distinctive methodological virtues and advantages of laboratory experiments in economics?
papers.method: Conceptual and methodological review synthesizing arguments for lab experimentation across control, causal inference, replication, and theory testing
papers.keyFinding: Laboratory experiments offer unique advantages including precise control over incentives and environment, clean causal identification, ability to test theoretical predictions, and a foundation for replication that field and observational methods cannot fully replicate
papers.whyItMatters: Defends the continued relevance and scientific value of lab experiments amid growing emphasis on field experiments and natural experiments, providing a methodological anchor for experimental economics

papers.title: A generalization of von Neumann’s reduction from the assignment problem to zero-sum games
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Ilan Adler, Martin Bullinger, Vijay V. Vazirani
papers.rq: Can the classical von Neumann reduction from the assignment problem to zero-sum games be generalized to broader classes of matching and optimization problems?
papers.method: Theoretical/mathematical analysis extending von Neumann's algebraic reduction technique to generalized assignment and matching frameworks, with connections to linear programming duality and game-theoretic equilibria.
papers.keyFinding: The authors successfully generalize von Neumann's reduction, showing that a wider class of assignment and combinatorial optimization problems can be embedded into zero-sum game structures, preserving solution equivalences and expanding the scope of game-theoretic methods in optimization.
papers.whyItMatters: This deepens the mathematical foundations linking optimization and game theory, potentially enabling new algorithmic approaches to matching markets and assignment problems by leveraging zero-sum game solvers.

papers.title: A model of participatory persuasion
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Liuchun Deng, Yufeng Sun

papers.title: A simultaneous analysis of turnout and voting under proportional representation: Theory and experiments
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Aaron Kamm, Arthur Schram
papers.rq: How do voters decide both whether to turn out and which candidate to vote for under proportional representation, and can equilibrium theory predict these joint decisions?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic modeling of simultaneous turnout and vote choice under PR, combined with controlled laboratory experiments to test equilibrium predictions
papers.keyFinding: Voter behavior under PR reflects strategic interaction between turnout and vote choice decisions; experimental results show partial support for equilibrium predictions but reveal systematic deviations, particularly in turnout levels and minority-party support
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding joint turnout and voting decisions under PR is essential for electoral system design and predicting political representation outcomes; most prior work treats these decisions separately

papers.title: Adapting stable matchings to evolving preferences
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Robert Bredereck, Jiehua Chen, Dušan Knop, Junjie Luo, Rolf Niedermeier
papers.rq: How can stable matchings be efficiently updated when agent preferences change over time?
papers.method: Computational complexity analysis and parameterized algorithm design for dynamic stable matching problems
papers.keyFinding: Adapting an existing stable matching to remain stable after preference changes is computationally tractable under certain parameterized conditions, with efficient algorithms identified for bounded numbers of preference changes or affected agents
papers.whyItMatters: Real-world matching markets (labor, school choice, dating) have evolving preferences; understanding when and how stable matchings can be repaired without full recomputation saves cost and reduces disruption

papers.title: Algorithmic collusion and a folk theorem from learning with bounded rationality
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Álvaro Cartea, Patrick Chang, José Penalva, Harrison Waldon
papers.rq: Can boundedly rational learning algorithms sustain collusive outcomes in repeated games, and under what conditions does a folk-theorem-style result emerge?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic modeling combining repeated game analysis with bounded rationality and algorithmic learning frameworks to derive conditions under which learning agents converge to collusive equilibria
papers.keyFinding: Boundedly rational learning algorithms can sustain supra-competitive prices akin to a folk theorem result, meaning collusion emerges endogenously from algorithmic learning without explicit coordination or programming to collude
papers.whyItMatters: Raises serious antitrust concerns for markets where pricing algorithms are prevalent, suggesting existing competition law may be inadequate to address collusion that arises spontaneously from algorithmic learning rather than explicit agreement

papers.title: Algorithms and complexity for computing Nash equilibria in adversarial team games
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Ioannis Anagnostides, Fivos Kalogiannis, Ioannis Panageas, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Stephen Mcaleer
papers.rq: How can Nash equilibria be efficiently computed in adversarial team games where a team of players faces an adversary?
papers.method: Theoretical computer science analysis combining game-theoretic modeling with complexity theory and algorithm design for adversarial team games
papers.keyFinding: The authors establish the computational complexity of finding Nash equilibria in adversarial team games and develop algorithms that exploit the team structure, identifying tractable cases and hardness boundaries for equilibrium computation
papers.whyItMatters: Adversarial team games model real-world scenarios like cybersecurity, military strategy, and competitive AI; understanding when equilibria can be computed efficiently has direct implications for multi-agent AI systems and mechanism design

papers.title: An experimental study of prisoners' dilemma and stag hunt games played by teams of players
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Jeongbin Kim, Thomas R. Palfrey
papers.rq: Do teams of players cooperate more or less than individuals in Prisoners' Dilemma and Stag Hunt games, and how does team decision-making affect coordination and cooperation outcomes?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment comparing individual versus team (multi-player) decision-making in Prisoners' Dilemma and Stag Hunt games, using controlled sessions to isolate the effect of team deliberation on strategic choices
papers.keyFinding: Teams tend to behave more strategically and self-interestedly than individuals in Prisoners' Dilemma games, leading to lower cooperation rates, while in Stag Hunt games teams show improved coordination on the payoff-dominant equilibrium through deliberation
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding whether collective deliberation enhances or undermines cooperation has direct implications for organizational design, committee decision-making, and policy contexts where group rather than individual choices determine social outcomes

papers.title: Approximating competitive equilibrium by Nash welfare
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jugal Garg, Yixin Tao, László A. Végh
papers.rq: How well can Nash welfare maximization approximate competitive equilibrium outcomes in exchange economies?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using algorithmic game theory and mathematical programming to bound the distance between Nash welfare-maximizing allocations and competitive equilibrium allocations
papers.keyFinding: Nash welfare maximization provides a provably good approximation to competitive equilibrium, with formal bounds characterizing how close the two solution concepts are across relevant classes of economies
papers.whyItMatters: Competitive equilibrium is computationally hard to find exactly; if Nash welfare—which is easier to optimize—approximates it well, this offers a practical algorithmic pathway for fair and efficient resource allocation

papers.title: Auction design with ambiguity: Optimality of the first-price auction
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Sung-Ha Hwang, Youngwoo Koh, Sosung Baik
papers.rq: What auction format is optimal when bidders face ambiguity about the valuation distribution rather than having precise probabilistic beliefs?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis using maxmin expected utility framework with ambiguity-averse bidders
papers.keyFinding: The first-price auction is optimal among a broad class of auction mechanisms when bidders are ambiguity-averse, reversing or qualifying the standard revenue-equivalence results that favor second-price or Vickrey auctions under risk neutrality
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the conventional wisdom that second-price auctions are dominant; suggests real-world auction designers should prefer first-price formats when bidders have Knightian uncertainty about rivals' valuations

papers.title: Authority measure for opinion dynamics
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Igal Milchtaich, Ron Peretz, Yevgeny Tsodikovich
papers.rq: How should authority or influence be formally measured among agents in opinion dynamics models?
papers.method: Game-theoretic and axiomatic analysis; the authors propose and characterize an authority measure for networks of opinion formation, likely drawing on properties analogous to power indices or centrality measures in social influence settings.
papers.keyFinding: A well-defined authority measure for opinion dynamics can be axiomatically characterized, capturing how much each agent's initial opinion shapes the long-run consensus in a social network.
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding who holds genuine authority in opinion-formation networks has implications for misinformation spread, political persuasion, and the design of deliberative institutions—offering a rigorous foundation for measuring social influence.

papers.title: Bayesian inference for Quantal Response Equilibrium in normal-form games
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): James R. Bland
papers.rq: How can Bayesian inference be applied to estimate Quantal Response Equilibrium (QRE) parameters in normal-form games?
papers.method: Bayesian statistical framework for estimating QRE models, applying posterior inference to normal-form game data
papers.keyFinding: Bayesian inference provides a principled and tractable approach to estimating QRE parameters, offering uncertainty quantification and improved model comparison over classical maximum likelihood methods
papers.whyItMatters: QRE is a leading model of bounded rationality in games; better estimation tools improve empirical testing of behavioral game theory and policy-relevant predictions about how real people play strategic situations

papers.title: Bureaucratic Norms and Dynamic Bayesian Persuasion
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 30 May 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Yihang Zhou

papers.title: Caps on bids in all-pay contests with identity-dependent externalities
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Dan Kovenock, Jian Song, Francesco Trevisan
papers.rq: How do caps on bids affect equilibrium behavior and outcomes in all-pay contests when players impose identity-dependent externalities on each other?
papers.method: Game-theoretic modeling of all-pay auctions/contests with bid caps and identity-dependent externalities, deriving and analyzing Nash equilibria analytically
papers.keyFinding: Bid caps in all-pay contests with identity-dependent externalities can alter equilibrium strategies non-trivially; the identity of who wins matters to losers, and caps interact with these externalities to shape effort levels, revenue, and efficiency in ways that differ from standard all-pay settings
papers.whyItMatters: Informs design of contests such as lobbying, R&D races, and political campaigns where the stakes depend not just on winning but on who the opponent is, helping policymakers set optimal bid or spending limits

papers.title: Cheap talk and lie detection
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 28 March 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Hitoshi Sadakane, Yin Chi Tam
papers.rq: Can a receiver improve information transmission in cheap talk by employing a lie detector that imperfectly identifies deception?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model of cheap talk with a lie detector that detects lies with some probability, analyzing equilibrium communication strategies between an informed sender and a receiver
papers.keyFinding: Introducing an imperfect lie detector can enhance information transmission relative to standard cheap talk, but the benefits depend critically on detection accuracy and the degree of preference misalignment between sender and receiver; in some cases the lie detector can fully unravel strategic deception
papers.whyItMatters: Informs the design of verification and auditing mechanisms in settings like regulation, negotiations, and political communication where costless deception is possible but perfect verification is infeasible

papers.title: Compellingness in Nash implementation
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shurojit Chatterji, Takashi Kunimoto, Paulo Ramos
papers.rq: What makes a Nash-implementing mechanism 'compelling' and how does this concept refine or restrict the set of implementable social choice rules?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis; formal game-theoretic framework introducing a compellingness criterion to evaluate Nash-implementing mechanisms and characterize which social choice correspondences satisfy it
papers.keyFinding: Not all social choice correspondences that are Nash implementable satisfy the compellingness criterion; the concept imposes additional discipline on equilibrium selection within implementing mechanisms, narrowing the class of admissible mechanisms and tightening implementation conditions beyond Maskin monotonicity
papers.whyItMatters: Addresses a longstanding weakness in Nash implementation theory—that mechanisms may have many equilibria, not all desirable—by providing a principled refinement that makes implementation more credible and practically meaningful for institutional design

papers.title: Competing for influence in networks through strategic targeting
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Margherita Comola, Agnieszka Rusinowska, Marie Claire Villeval
papers.rq: How do competing agents strategically target individuals in a network to maximize their influence over the broader population?
papers.method: Game-theoretic model of network influence competition, where players choose targeting strategies over nodes, combined with experimental or analytical characterization of equilibrium behavior in network structures.
papers.keyFinding: Strategic targeting equilibria depend critically on network topology; competing influencers tend to focus on central or bridging nodes, and the structure of competition leads to predictable patterns of over- or under-investment in influence relative to social optimum.
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals how political campaigns, advertisers, or lobbyists allocate persuasion resources across networked populations, informing policy on information spread, polarization, and the design of platforms or networks resistant to manipulation.

papers.title: Competition in persuasion in the attention economy
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 24 April 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Federico Innocenti
papers.rq: How does competition among senders affect persuasion outcomes when a receiver has limited attention?
papers.method: Game-theoretic model of Bayesian persuasion with multiple competing senders and an attention-constrained receiver
papers.keyFinding: Competition in persuasion under limited attention leads to senders designing more extreme or polarized information structures to capture the receiver's attention, potentially reducing overall information quality compared to monopoly persuasion
papers.whyItMatters: As digital platforms and media compete for scarce consumer attention, understanding how this competition shapes the informativeness and bias of messages has direct implications for regulation, platform design, and welfare

papers.title: Competitive limit of competing auctions
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Zizhen Ma, Nicolás Riquelme
papers.rq: Do competing auctions converge to competitive (Walrasian) equilibrium outcomes as markets grow large?
papers.method: Theoretical model of decentralized competing auctions with strategic buyers and sellers; analyzes equilibrium behavior in the limit as the number of market participants grows large
papers.keyFinding: Competing auctions achieve the competitive limit: as the market grows thick, equilibrium prices and allocations converge to Walrasian equilibrium outcomes, resolving inefficiencies from strategic bidding and market fragmentation
papers.whyItMatters: Provides theoretical justification for decentralized auction markets as efficient allocation mechanisms at scale, with implications for platform design, financial markets, and procurement

papers.title: Conventions in large games with randomly drawn payoffs
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Jonathan Newton, Ryoji Sawa
papers.rq: How do conventions (stochastically stable equilibria) emerge in large games when payoffs are drawn randomly from a distribution?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis combining stochastic stability and evolutionary game theory; examines large-population normal-form games with randomly assigned payoffs and analyzes long-run equilibrium selection under noise-driven learning dynamics.
papers.keyFinding: In large games with randomly drawn payoffs, risk-dominant or payoff-dominant conventions emerge with high probability; the structure of randomly assigned payoffs shapes which equilibria are selected as stochastically stable, and results generalize equilibrium selection principles to settings where payoff heterogeneity is the norm rather than the exception.
papers.whyItMatters: Many real-world coordination problems involve agents with heterogeneous, privately known payoffs; this paper provides theoretical foundations for predicting which social conventions will emerge in such environments, extending classical equilibrium selection results beyond symmetric or known-payoff settings.

papers.title: Delay in social learning
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Moritz Meyer-ter-Vehn

papers.title: Designing Heaven’s will: The job assignment in the Chinese imperial civil service
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Inácio Bó, Li Chen
papers.rq: How did the Chinese imperial civil service design its job assignment mechanism, and what were its strategic and efficiency properties?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis of historical Chinese imperial civil service assignment rules, likely modeling the placement of examination graduates into official positions
papers.keyFinding: The imperial Chinese civil service used an assignment mechanism with specific strategic properties; the paper characterizes how 'Heaven's will' randomization and rank-based assignment interacted to produce (or fail to produce) incentive-compatible and efficient outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Provides historical grounding for modern matching and assignment theory, showing that sophisticated mechanism design principles were embedded in pre-modern institutions, with implications for understanding the origins and robustness of assignment mechanisms

papers.title: Duality in financial networks
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Martijn W. Ketelaars, Peter Borm, P. Jean-Jacques Herings
papers.rq: What dual structure underlies financial network clearing problems and how can it be exploited analytically?
papers.method: Cooperative game theory and convex duality applied to financial network models with bilateral debt obligations, deriving dual representations of clearing payment vectors and value functions
papers.keyFinding: Financial network clearing problems exhibit a formal duality structure: the primal problem of finding clearing payment vectors has a dual whose solutions characterize shadow prices of liquidity, enabling unified treatment of existence, uniqueness, and comparative statics of equilibria
papers.whyItMatters: Duality provides a powerful analytical lens for systemic risk analysis, simplifying proofs of core results and potentially guiding policy on how liquidity injections or debt restructuring propagate through interconnected financial systems

papers.title: Efficient equilibrium in submodular global games of entry
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Rabah Amir, Rodrigo Harrison, Pedro Jara-Moroni
papers.rq: Under what conditions does an efficient equilibrium exist in global games of market entry with strategic complementarities and submodular payoffs?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using global games framework with submodular payoff functions and equilibrium selection techniques
papers.keyFinding: An efficient equilibrium exists in submodular global games of entry, where the equilibrium selected via global games refinement coincides with the socially optimal outcome, resolving coordination failures under specific payoff conditions
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies when decentralized entry decisions lead to efficient market outcomes without coordination mechanisms, with implications for industrial organization and market design

papers.title: Electoral accountability in the lab
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): César Martinelli, Naila C. Sebastián Esandi
papers.rq: Do voters effectively hold politicians accountable through elections, and how do strategic incentives shape electoral behavior in controlled settings?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment using game-theoretic electoral accountability frameworks, testing voter and politician behavior under controlled incentive structures
papers.keyFinding: Voters exhibit limited but meaningful accountability behavior; politicians respond to electoral incentives but strategic considerations and information frictions reduce the efficiency of accountability mechanisms compared to theoretical benchmarks
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the behavioral foundations of electoral accountability is critical for democratic design; lab evidence reveals where theory succeeds and fails in predicting real-world voting and political behavior

papers.title: Eliciting and distinguishing between weak and incomplete preferences: Theory, experiment and computation
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 26 May 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Georgios Gerasimou

papers.title: Endogenous barriers to learning
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Olivier Compte
papers.rq: Can rational agents fail to learn the truth even with unlimited data, due to self-generated barriers in their information acquisition or updating process?
papers.method: Theoretical model using game-theoretic and decision-theoretic frameworks to analyze endogenous information structures and Bayesian updating under self-selected evidence
papers.keyFinding: Agents can endogenously create barriers to learning by selectively engaging with information in ways that confirm prior beliefs, leading to persistent belief distortions even in the long run; the barriers arise from within the agent's own optimization rather than external constraints
papers.whyItMatters: Explains why rational-seeming agents persistently hold wrong beliefs, with implications for markets, policy, and mechanism design where information provision alone may not correct misbeliefs

papers.title: Equilibrium cycle: A “Dynamic” equilibrium
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Tushar Shankar Walunj, Shiksha Singhal, Veeraruna Kavitha, Jayakrishnan Nair
papers.rq: Can dynamic, cycling behavior among agents constitute a stable equilibrium concept in game theory?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis introducing a new solution concept called 'equilibrium cycle,' which formalizes recurrent strategic dynamics as an equilibrium rather than a static fixed point.
papers.keyFinding: The authors establish an 'equilibrium cycle' concept that captures self-sustaining cyclic behavior in games as a legitimate dynamic equilibrium, providing existence conditions and characterizing when agents rationally perpetuate cycling rather than converging to a static Nash equilibrium.
papers.whyItMatters: Many real-world strategic interactions exhibit persistent cycling rather than settling at fixed points; this framework legitimizes and analyzes such dynamics, potentially explaining phenomena in markets, routing, and repeated competition that classical equilibrium concepts cannot.

papers.title: Evaluating non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms: Theory and experiment
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shan Gui, Daniel Houser
papers.rq: How well do non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms perform relative to optimal benchmarks, and do real decision-makers behave as theory predicts within them?
papers.method: Combination of theoretical mechanism design analysis and laboratory experiment; participants interact with dynamic mechanisms that lack foresight about future agent types
papers.keyFinding: Non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms achieve strong efficiency and revenue properties in theory, but laboratory subjects systematically deviate from equilibrium predictions, revealing behavioral frictions that erode theoretical performance gains
papers.whyItMatters: Dynamic mechanism design is central to real-world applications like auctions, procurement, and platform pricing; understanding the gap between theoretical and actual performance informs more robust mechanism construction

papers.title: Failing to correctly aggregate signals
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Michele Piccione, Ariel Rubinstein
papers.rq: How do individuals fail to correctly aggregate multiple signals when forming beliefs or making decisions?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic and decision-theoretic modeling using bounded rationality frameworks to analyze signal aggregation errors
papers.keyFinding: Individuals systematically fail to correctly combine multiple pieces of information into coherent beliefs, making predictable aggregation errors that deviate from Bayesian updating in structured ways
papers.whyItMatters: Signal aggregation is fundamental to markets, voting, and expert judgment; understanding systematic failures helps explain anomalies in collective decision-making and individual inference

papers.title: Guilt and fairness
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Alessandro Stringhi
papers.rq: How does guilt influence fairness preferences and behavior in strategic interactions?
papers.method: Theoretical model incorporating guilt aversion into a game-theoretic framework to analyze how anticipated guilt shapes players' fairness-related decisions
papers.keyFinding: Guilt aversion generates endogenous fairness concerns: players who dislike letting others down behave as if they have fairness preferences, producing outcomes consistent with fair division even in the absence of intrinsic equity motives
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a unified psychological microfoundation linking guilt to observed fairness behavior, suggesting that guilt—rather than inequality aversion—may drive many experimental results on fair division and cooperation

papers.title: High-stakes failures of backward induction
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Bouke Klein Teeselink, Dennie van Dolder, Martijn J. van den Assem, Jason D. Dana
papers.rq: Do people apply backward induction correctly in high-stakes, real-world sequential games?
papers.method: Empirical analysis of natural experiments using data from high-stakes TV game shows featuring sequential decision problems where backward induction yields clear optimal strategies
papers.keyFinding: Contestants systematically fail to apply backward induction even when stakes are extremely high, making suboptimal decisions that cannot be explained by risk preferences or confusion alone, suggesting the failure is robust and not merely a lab artifact
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the assumption that high stakes discipline behavior toward rationality; backward induction failures persist outside the lab, undermining a core solution concept in game theory and raising questions about strategic reasoning in real economic decisions

papers.title: Information Manipulation of Wishful Thinkers
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 25 May 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Emel Filiz-Ozbay, Zhenxun Liu
papers.rq: How do information senders strategically manipulate wishful thinkers who derive utility from beliefs themselves?
papers.method: Theoretical model combining Bayesian persuasion with wishful thinking agents who have belief-based utility
papers.keyFinding: Senders exploit wishful thinkers by strategically withholding negative information, leading to more optimistic but less accurate beliefs; the equilibrium information structure differs substantially from that targeting rational agents
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals how motivated reasoning and belief-based utility create exploitable vulnerabilities in information environments, with implications for advertising, political communication, and financial advice

papers.title: Introduction to 25+ years of quantal response equilibrium
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Marco Battaglini, Thomas R. Palfrey
papers.rq: What have 25+ years of quantal response equilibrium (QRE) research contributed to economics and game theory?
papers.method: Retrospective survey and editorial introduction reviewing theoretical developments and empirical applications of QRE since its introduction
papers.keyFinding: QRE has become a foundational framework for modeling boundedly rational strategic behavior, generating substantial theoretical extensions and empirical applications across economics, political science, and related fields over more than two decades
papers.whyItMatters: QRE bridges classical equilibrium theory and behavioral economics by allowing for systematic decision errors, providing a tractable alternative to Nash equilibrium that better fits experimental and real-world data

papers.title: Istanbul flower auction: The need for speed
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Isa Hafalir, Onur Kesten, Donglai Luo, Katerina Sherstyuk, Cong Tao
papers.rq: How does auction speed affect bidding behavior and outcomes in a descending-price (Dutch) flower auction setting?
papers.method: Field and/or laboratory experiment analyzing the Istanbul flower auction, likely combining structural estimation or experimental manipulation of auction pace
papers.keyFinding: Auction speed is a critical design parameter in Dutch auctions; faster auctions systematically affect bidder behavior and market efficiency, with implications for optimal auction design in time-pressured environments
papers.whyItMatters: Flower auctions are high-stakes, real-world Dutch auction mechanisms handling perishable goods under extreme time pressure; understanding speed effects informs better market design for commodity and perishable-goods markets globally

papers.title: Justified-envy-minimal efficient mechanisms for priority-based matching
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Hyukjun Kwon, Ran I. Shorrer
papers.rq: What mechanisms achieve efficiency in priority-based matching while minimizing justified envy among agents?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis; axiomatic characterization of matching mechanisms that satisfy efficiency and minimize justified envy subject to that efficiency constraint
papers.keyFinding: The authors characterize mechanisms that are both efficient and minimize justified envy, identifying the structure of justified-envy-minimal efficient mechanisms in priority-based matching markets such as school choice
papers.whyItMatters: School choice and similar assignment markets face a fundamental tension between efficiency and fairness (justified envy); this paper clarifies the frontier of that tradeoff, informing policymakers on how to design assignment systems that are as fair as possible without sacrificing efficiency

papers.title: Lucky but confident –The effect of confidence on meritocratic beliefs and preferences for redistribution
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Kajsa Hansson, Oda Kristine Storstad Sund
papers.rq: Does individual confidence level affect meritocratic beliefs and willingness to redistribute, even when outcomes are determined by luck?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment in which participants receive luck-based outcomes but are randomly assigned to high or low confidence conditions, then report meritocratic beliefs and redistribution preferences
papers.keyFinding: Higher confidence causes individuals to attribute luck-based success to personal merit and reduces their support for redistribution, suggesting confidence distorts the perceived link between effort and outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals a psychological mechanism by which self-confidence—independent of actual performance—shapes inequality acceptance and redistributive politics, with implications for understanding why meritocratic narratives persist even in unequal societies

papers.title: Morality meets risk: What makes a good excuse for selfishness
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Wanxin Dong, Jiakun Zheng
papers.rq: What types of excuses allow individuals to justify selfish behavior in moral decision-making contexts, and what characteristics make an excuse effective?
papers.method: Theoretical model combined with laboratory experiments examining how individuals use available excuses to rationalize selfish choices in dictator and risk-based games
papers.keyFinding: Excuses are more effective at enabling selfish behavior when they introduce plausible deniability through risk or ambiguity; moral wiggle room is most powerful when it allows agents to attribute selfish outcomes to chance or uncertainty rather than deliberate choice
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the conditions under which people exploit moral loopholes has implications for contract design, charitable giving, corporate accountability, and policy interventions aimed at reducing socially harmful self-interested behavior

papers.title: Motives for Delegating Financial Decisions
