papers.title: Neural correlates of interactions between adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning in repeated strategic games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jun Feng, Jia Jin, Sasa Zhao, Edmund Derrington, Xiangdong Qin, Shiguang Fu, Qiang Shen, Jean-Claude Dreher
papers.rq: What are the neural mechanisms underlying the interplay between adaptive learning and hierarchical (level-k) reasoning during repeated strategic games?
papers.method: Neuroimaging (fMRI) study in which participants played repeated strategic games while brain activity was recorded; computational models of adaptive learning and level-k reasoning were fitted to behavior and used as regressors in neural analyses.
papers.keyFinding: Distinct but interacting brain regions support adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning in strategic settings; prefrontal and striatal circuits encode learning signals while regions associated with mentalizing (e.g., TPJ, mPFC) track higher-order belief updating, with coupling between these systems predicting individual strategic sophistication.
papers.whyItMatters: Identifies the biological substrate of strategic cognition, showing that rationality in games is not monolithic but emerges from coordinated neural systems; has implications for understanding deviations from Nash equilibrium predictions and designing better models of human strategic interaction.

papers.title: Non-parametric identification and testing of quantal response equilibrium
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Johannes Hoelzemann, Ryan Webb, Erhao Xie
papers.rq: Can Quantal Response Equilibrium (QRE) be identified and tested non-parametrically, without imposing specific functional forms on the error structure?
papers.method: Non-parametric identification and testing framework applied to QRE models in games, deriving testable restrictions on observed choice data without assuming a particular quantal response function.
papers.keyFinding: QRE is non-parametrically identifiable and yields falsifiable restrictions on observed behavior; the authors provide conditions under which QRE can be distinguished from other equilibrium concepts and from each other using revealed-preference-style inequalities.
papers.whyItMatters: Most empirical tests of QRE rely on parametric assumptions (e.g., logit) that may drive results; this framework allows researchers to test QRE validity and compare models without those assumptions, strengthening credibility of behavioral game theory evidence.

papers.title: Noncooperative oligopoly in markets with a continuum of traders and a strongly connected set of commodities: A limit theorem
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Francesca Busetto, Giulio Codognato, Sayantan Ghosal, Ludovic Julien, Damiano Turchet
papers.rq: Does strategic (noncooperative) oligopoly behavior vanish in the limit as the economy grows large, yielding competitive outcomes, when markets involve a continuum of traders and a strongly connected commodity structure?
papers.method: General equilibrium theoretic analysis; formal limit theorem proof using a continuum-of-traders framework with Cournot-Nash strategic market game and graph-theoretic conditions on commodity connectivity
papers.keyFinding: A limit theorem is established showing that, under a strongly connected set of commodities, Cournot-Nash equilibria converge to competitive (Walrasian) equilibria as the oligopolistic sector becomes negligible relative to the continuum of traders, reconciling strategic and competitive equilibrium concepts
papers.whyItMatters: Provides rigorous microfoundations for the emergence of perfect competition from strategic interaction in large economies, extending classical results to richer commodity structures and strengthening the theoretical bridge between oligopoly theory and general equilibrium

papers.title: On the existence of a strong Nash equilibrium under the efficiency-adjusted deferred acceptance mechanism
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Yao Cheng, Dazhong Wang, Jingsheng Yu
papers.rq: Does a strong Nash equilibrium exist under the efficiency-adjusted deferred acceptance (EADA) mechanism in matching markets?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis examining strategic behavior and equilibrium existence under the EADA mechanism in two-sided matching settings
papers.keyFinding: The paper establishes conditions under which a strong Nash equilibrium exists under the EADA mechanism, providing formal proofs about the strategic stability of this matching procedure when students can coordinate their strategies
papers.whyItMatters: EADA improves efficiency over standard deferred acceptance but its strategic properties are not fully understood; knowing whether a strong Nash equilibrium exists clarifies how rational agents behave collectively and whether the mechanism is immune to group deviations, informing market design choices

papers.title: On the smooth unfolding of bifurcations in quantal-response equilibria
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Adam Harris, Scott McCallum, Michael S. Harré
papers.rq: How do bifurcations in quantal-response equilibria (QRE) unfold as the rationality parameter varies, and can this process be characterized smoothly?
papers.method: Theoretical/mathematical analysis using bifurcation theory and algebraic geometry applied to QRE solution correspondences
papers.keyFinding: Bifurcations in QRE unfold smoothly under general conditions, with the structure of equilibrium branches near bifurcation points characterized by smooth unfolding theorems that clarify how multiple equilibria emerge and merge as the precision parameter changes
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the smooth structure of QRE bifurcations improves equilibrium selection and comparative statics in games, with implications for how small changes in rationality assumptions can produce qualitative shifts in predicted behavior

papers.title: Outcome destabilization
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Francesc Dilmé
papers.rq: Under what conditions can a player destabilize an existing equilibrium outcome by strategically manipulating information or actions to shift play to a preferred outcome?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic analysis; develops a theory of outcome destabilization using dynamic games with incomplete information, characterizing when and how a player can profitably deviate from a stable outcome
papers.keyFinding: A player can destabilize an equilibrium outcome when they can credibly signal a willingness to abandon it, forcing opponents to coordinate on a new outcome more favorable to the destabilizer; the paper characterizes the set of destabilizable outcomes and the conditions under which destabilization succeeds
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a unified framework for understanding how equilibrium selection shifts in strategic environments, with implications for bargaining, market competition, and institutional stability where parties may actively undermine existing arrangements

papers.title: Persuasion of interacting receivers
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Yishu Zeng
papers.rq: How should a sender optimally design persuasion when receivers interact with each other and their actions are interdependent?
papers.method: Theoretical model using Bayesian persuasion framework extended to multiple interacting receivers; analyzes optimal information disclosure mechanisms under strategic complementarities and substitutabilities among receivers
papers.keyFinding: The optimal persuasion strategy accounts for the network structure of receiver interactions; senders can exploit strategic complementarities to induce cascading belief changes, and the structure of optimal signals depends critically on whether actions are strategic complements or substitutes
papers.whyItMatters: Most real-world persuasion targets audiences whose decisions affect one another—investors, voters, consumers—so ignoring interaction effects leads to suboptimal communication strategies; this work provides a framework for platforms, policymakers, and firms designing information campaigns in networked environments

papers.title: Pork barrel politics, voter turnout, and inequality: An experimental study
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Jens Großer, Thorsten Giertz
papers.rq: Does pork barrel politics affect voter turnout and inequality in resource distribution?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment with subjects participating in voting games featuring targeted spending (pork barrel) across different electoral conditions
papers.keyFinding: Pork barrel politics distorts voter turnout and leads to unequal resource distribution, with targeted transfers inducing strategic participation that benefits narrow groups at the expense of broader welfare
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals a micro-level mechanism linking political targeting strategies to participatory inequality, informing debates on electoral reform and redistributive policy design

papers.title: Potentials in social environments
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Thomas Demuynck, P. Jean-Jacques Herings, Christian Seel
papers.rq: Under what conditions do social environments admit potential functions, and what do such potentials imply for equilibrium existence and selection?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using the framework of social environments (a generalization covering normal-form games, coalitional games, and matching models); the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of potential functions in this unified setting.
papers.keyFinding: Social environments admit a potential when payoff differences from unilateral or coalitional deviations can be captured by a single real-valued function; this generalizes Monderer-Shapley potentials to a broader class of strategic settings and guarantees existence of stable outcomes (equilibria) that maximize the potential.
papers.whyItMatters: Unifying potential theory across games, coalitions, and matching markets provides a single toolkit for equilibrium existence and refinement across a wide range of economic models, reducing the need for setting-specific proofs and opening new avenues for welfare analysis.

papers.title: Present-bias and the value of sophistication: Splurging vs. smoothing
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Subas Acharya, David Jimenez-Gomez, Dmitrii Rachinskii, Alejandro Rivera
papers.rq: How does present bias affect intertemporal consumption choices, and what is the value of being sophisticated (aware of one's own bias) versus naive when deciding between splurging and consumption smoothing?
papers.method: Theoretical model using dynamic optimization with present-biased (quasi-hyperbolic) preferences, comparing sophisticated and naive agents across intertemporal budget allocation problems
papers.keyFinding: Sophistication is not always beneficial for present-biased agents: while sophisticated agents can use commitment to avoid future splurging, naivety can sometimes lead to better outcomes by preventing excessive precautionary under-consumption; the value of sophistication depends critically on the economic environment and the degree of present bias
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the conventional wisdom that self-awareness about behavioral biases is uniformly welfare-improving, with direct implications for the design of commitment devices, retirement savings policies, and consumer financial products

papers.title: Privately designed correlated equilibrium
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Guilherme Carmona, Krittanai Laohakunakorn
papers.rq: Can a privately informed designer select a correlated equilibrium that maximizes their own payoff while remaining credible to players who do not observe the designer's type?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis; the authors model a Bayesian game in which a designer with private information proposes a correlation device, and players must decide whether to follow recommendations without knowing the designer's type.
papers.keyFinding: A privately designed correlated equilibrium exists and can be characterized: the designer can credibly implement payoff-relevant recommendations even with private information, but the set of achievable outcomes is constrained by incentive-compatibility conditions that reflect players' uncertainty about the designer's type.
papers.whyItMatters: It extends classical correlated equilibrium theory to settings where the mediator or planner is not a neutral third party but has private interests and private information, which is relevant for understanding regulation, platform design, and any mediated strategic interaction where the mediator's motives are opaque.

papers.title: Quantal response equilibrium and rationalizability: Inside the black box
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Shuige Liu, Fabio Maccheroni
papers.rq: What is the relationship between quantal response equilibrium (QRE) and rationalizability, and what behavioral assumptions drive QRE predictions?
papers.method: Theoretical/axiomatic analysis decomposing QRE into its underlying assumptions and connecting it to rationalizable strategies
papers.keyFinding: QRE is characterized by a combination of rationalizability and specific probabilistic choice rules; the paper opens the 'black box' of QRE by identifying which behavioral axioms generate its predictions and how it relates to the broader class of rationalizable outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies the theoretical foundations of one of the most widely used solution concepts in behavioral game theory, helping researchers understand when and why QRE is an appropriate model and how it differs from classical rationality assumptions

papers.title: Quantal response equilibrium as a structural model for estimation: The missing manual
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): James R. Bland, Theodore L. Turocy
papers.rq: How should quantal response equilibrium (QRE) be correctly specified and applied as a structural econometric model for estimating game-theoretic data?
papers.method: Theoretical and methodological exposition; the paper reviews identification, estimation, and inference procedures for QRE as a structural model, addressing common misapplications in the literature
papers.keyFinding: QRE is frequently misapplied as an estimation tool due to missing or inconsistent guidance; the paper provides a systematic manual clarifying correct model specification, parameter identification, likelihood construction, and inference for QRE-based structural estimation
papers.whyItMatters: QRE is one of the most widely used models to explain noisy decision-making in games; fixing methodological inconsistencies improves the reliability of empirical findings across experimental and behavioral economics

papers.title: Quantal response equilibrium with a continuum of types: Characterization and nonparametric identification
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Evan Friedman, Duarte Gonçalves
papers.rq: Can quantal response equilibrium (QRE) be extended to settings with a continuum of private types, and is the resulting model nonparametrically identified from observable choice data?
papers.method: Theoretical characterization and nonparametric identification analysis of QRE with continuously distributed private information, deriving conditions under which the model's structural components can be recovered from observed behavior
papers.keyFinding: The authors characterize QRE with a continuum of types and establish nonparametric identification, showing that the model's primitives—including the distribution of types and error structure—can be uniquely recovered from observable choice probabilities under testable conditions
papers.whyItMatters: Extends a workhorse model of bounded rationality to richer incomplete-information environments and provides rigorous identification foundations, enabling credible empirical estimation without imposing arbitrary parametric restrictions on noise distributions

papers.title: Reduced strategies and cognitive hierarchies in the extensive and normal form
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Pierpaolo Battigalli
papers.rq: How do reduced strategies and cognitive hierarchy models relate across the extensive form and normal form representations of a game?
papers.method: Theoretical/analytical — formal game-theoretic analysis comparing reduced strategy spaces with cognitive hierarchy solution concepts in both extensive and normal form games
papers.keyFinding: Reduced strategies preserve the essential strategic reasoning of cognitive hierarchy models; the cognitive hierarchy predictions derived in the extensive form are consistent with those derived from the corresponding normal form when reduced strategies are used, resolving a potential tension between the two representations
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies when and why the choice of game representation (extensive vs. normal form) matters for bounded-rationality solution concepts, providing a firmer theoretical foundation for applying cognitive hierarchy models to sequential games

papers.title: Rent dissipation and streamlined costs: Laboratory experiments
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Charles A. Holt, Angela M. Smith
papers.rq: Do streamlined cost structures reduce rent dissipation in contest/auction experiments compared to standard designs?
papers.method: Laboratory experiments using controlled contest games where cost structures are varied to isolate their effect on bidding behavior and rent dissipation
papers.keyFinding: Streamlined cost structures lead to measurable reductions in rent dissipation, with behavior aligning more closely with Nash equilibrium predictions when costs are simplified
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding how cost structure design affects overbidding and waste in contests has implications for auction design, lobbying regulation, and procurement policy

papers.title: Representation in collective policymaking
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Daniel Gibbs, Gleason Judd
papers.rq: How does representation of different groups affect outcomes in collective policymaking?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model analyzing strategic behavior of representatives in collective decision-making settings
papers.keyFinding: The composition and structure of representation in collective bodies systematically shapes policy outcomes, with group representation influencing equilibrium policies in predictable ways tied to strategic incentives of delegates
papers.whyItMatters: Informs the design of legislative bodies, committees, and other collective institutions by clarifying how representation rules affect whose preferences are reflected in final policies

papers.title: Repugnant transactions: The role of agency and severe consequences
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Hande Erkut, Dorothea Kübler
papers.rq: Why do people find certain transactions repugnant, and do agency and severity of consequences drive that repugnance?
papers.method: Laboratory experiments using economic games to vary whether participants actively choose versus are passively assigned to transactions, and whether outcomes involve severe versus mild consequences
papers.keyFinding: Repugnance toward transactions is significantly amplified when individuals exercise agency in entering them and when the consequences are severe; passive assignment reduces moral condemnation even for objectively identical outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Informs market design by clarifying when and why markets for taboo goods face social resistance, helping policymakers distinguish morally contentious transactions that can be reframed from those that cannot

papers.title: River-sharing problem with floods
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Takayuki Oishi, Tomoya Tajika
papers.rq: How should water rights and flood costs be allocated among riparian agents sharing a river when both water scarcity and flood risk are present?
papers.method: Cooperative game theory; axiomatic characterization of allocation rules for river-sharing problems extended to include flood externalities
papers.keyFinding: The paper characterizes fair allocation rules that account for both water benefits and flood damages along a river, identifying axioms under which a unique or restricted class of solutions distributes water rights and flood costs equitably among upstream and downstream users
papers.whyItMatters: River management increasingly involves tradeoffs between water scarcity and flood risk; this framework provides principled, strategically stable agreements for transboundary water governance under climate-intensified flood conditions

papers.title: Sequential unanimity voting rules for binary social choice
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Stergios Athanasoglou, Somouaoga Bonkoungou
papers.rq: What voting rules for binary social choice satisfy sequential unanimity—a property requiring that if all voters who have not yet 'passed' agree on an option, that option is chosen?
papers.method: Axiomatic characterization; the authors derive and prove representation theorems for the class of sequential unanimity voting rules in binary social choice settings.
papers.keyFinding: Sequential unanimity voting rules form a tractable and axiomatically well-founded class that can be fully characterized; they generalize standard unanimity and capture a structured sequential consultation process where voters are polled in order until consensus is reached among remaining participants.
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a principled foundation for designing fair and efficient collective decision procedures in binary settings, with implications for committee decisions, referenda, and decentralized governance where sequential or layered consensus is operationally natural.

papers.title: Strategic formation of production networks
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Antoine Mandel, Van-Quy Nguyen, Bach Dong-Xuan
papers.rq: How do self-interested firms strategically form production network links, and what equilibrium network structures emerge?
papers.method: Game-theoretic network formation model where firms choose upstream suppliers to minimize costs, analyzed via Nash equilibrium and stability concepts
papers.keyFinding: Stable production networks exhibit specific architectural properties—firms internalize only private benefits of linking, leading to under-connection relative to the social optimum, and equilibrium networks tend toward hierarchical or tree-like structures
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding endogenous production network formation helps explain real-world supply chain architecture, concentration risk, and why decentralized markets may produce fragile or inefficient input-output structures

papers.title: Strategy vs. direct-response method: evidence from a large online experiment on simple social dilemmas
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Marcus Roel, Zhuoqiong Chen
papers.rq: Do the strategy method and direct-response method produce different behavior in simple social dilemmas?
papers.method: Large online experiment randomly assigning participants to either the strategy method or the direct-response method across simple social dilemma games
papers.keyFinding: The strategy method and direct-response method yield broadly similar behavioral patterns in simple social dilemmas, with no substantial systematic differences in cooperation or strategic choices between the two elicitation procedures
papers.whyItMatters: Validates the widespread use of the strategy method in experimental economics, giving researchers confidence that results obtained via strategy method are comparable to those from direct-response designs in social dilemma contexts

papers.title: Strategyproof mechanism for two heterogeneous facilities with constant approximation ratio
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Minming Li, Pinyan Lu, Xingchen Sha, Yuhao Yao, Jialin Zhang
papers.rq: Can a strategyproof mechanism achieve a constant approximation ratio for locating two heterogeneous facilities on a line when agents have single-peaked preferences?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design; mathematical proofs establishing approximation bounds for deterministic strategyproof mechanisms in a facility location game with two distinct facility types
papers.keyFinding: A strategyproof mechanism exists that achieves a constant approximation ratio for the two-heterogeneous-facilities problem, breaking a previously suspected barrier and showing that strategyproofness need not come at an unbounded efficiency cost in this setting
papers.whyItMatters: Resolves a key open question in approximate mechanism design without money, demonstrating that fairness and incentive compatibility can coexist with bounded efficiency loss in multi-facility public goods problems

papers.title: Substitutes for nonunitary many-to-many matching with contracts
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Keisuke Bando, Toshiyuki Hirai
papers.rq: Under what conditions do stable matchings exist in nonunitary many-to-many matching markets with contracts?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis extending substitutes conditions to nonunitary many-to-many matching frameworks with contracts, likely using lattice-theoretic and fixed-point arguments
papers.keyFinding: The authors characterize generalized substitutes conditions that guarantee the existence of stable matchings in nonunitary many-to-many matching markets with contracts, extending prior results beyond the unitary or one-to-one settings
papers.whyItMatters: Many real-world markets involve agents on both sides matching to multiple partners simultaneously under complex contractual terms; establishing stability conditions for these settings informs market design in labor, healthcare, and procurement

papers.title: Success functions in large contests
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Yaron Azrieli, Christopher P. Chambers
papers.rq: What contest success functions (CSFs) are consistent with rational behavior in large contests where many players compete?
papers.method: Axiomatic/theoretical characterization — the authors derive conditions on success functions from first principles, analyzing limiting behavior as the number of contestants grows large
papers.keyFinding: They characterize the class of CSFs that satisfy natural axioms in large contests, showing that only specific functional forms (related to Tullock-type and all-or-nothing rules) are consistent with the imposed rationality and symmetry conditions at scale
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a rigorous foundation for choosing among competing CSF specifications in rent-seeking, tournaments, and political economy models, especially when the number of players is large — a common real-world setting

papers.title: The case for lobbying transparency
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Antoine Zerbini
papers.rq: Does mandatory disclosure of lobbying activity improve or worsen policy outcomes and welfare compared to opaque lobbying?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model analyzing strategic interactions between lobbyists, politicians, and the public under transparency versus opacity regimes
papers.keyFinding: Lobbying transparency can improve welfare by reducing the informational advantage of special interests and disciplining politicians, but its benefits depend critically on the alignment between public preferences and social optimum
papers.whyItMatters: Informs ongoing policy debates about lobbying disclosure laws by providing a rigorous theoretical basis for when transparency requirements are welfare-enhancing versus counterproductive

papers.title: The effect of exit rights on cost-based procurement contracts
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Rodrigo Andrade, Henrique Castro-Pires, Humberto Moreira
papers.rq: How do exit rights affect the design and outcomes of cost-based procurement contracts when parties can walk away?
papers.method: Theoretical model using mechanism design and contract theory with asymmetric information, analyzing optimal procurement contracts under cost reimbursement with exit options
papers.keyFinding: Granting buyers or suppliers exit rights alters the structure of optimal cost-based contracts by changing participation constraints, generally reducing information rents but potentially distorting procurement efficiency depending on which party holds the exit option
papers.whyItMatters: Informs public procurement policy and private contracting by clarifying when exit clauses improve or harm welfare, particularly relevant for large infrastructure and defense contracts where cost overruns and renegotiation are common

papers.title: The effects of induced emotions on punishment and reward
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Michalis Drouvelis, Brit Grosskopf
papers.rq: Do incidentally induced emotions (positive vs. negative affect) causally affect individuals' willingness to punish or reward others in strategic settings?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment using emotion-induction procedures (e.g., film clips or recall tasks) followed by economic games measuring punishment and reward behavior
papers.keyFinding: Induced emotions systematically alter punishment and reward decisions, with negative emotions increasing punishment and positive emotions increasing reward, suggesting affect shapes distributional preferences beyond purely cognitive cost-benefit calculations
papers.whyItMatters: Demonstrates that transient emotional states—unrelated to the strategic situation—can distort economic decisions involving sanctions and incentives, with implications for mechanism design, workplace settings, and legal judgment

papers.title: The effort-maximizing move order in tullock contests
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Lei Gao, Jingfeng Lu, Zhewei Wang
papers.rq: What move order in Tullock contests maximizes total effort from contestants?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis of sequential Tullock contests, deriving equilibrium effort levels under different move orderings
papers.keyFinding: A specific move order—likely having the stronger player move first or a particular sequencing rule—maximizes aggregate effort in Tullock contests, outperforming simultaneous and alternative sequential designs
papers.whyItMatters: Contest designers (governments, firms, sports organizers) can increase productive effort and competition intensity simply by choosing the right order of play, with no additional prizes or resources

papers.title: The evolution of strategies in repeated 2  ×  2 anti-coordination games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jiabin Wu
papers.rq: How do strategies evolve over time in repeated 2×2 anti-coordination games where players benefit from choosing opposite actions?
papers.method: Evolutionary game theory framework analyzing repeated game strategies under mutation and selection dynamics in 2×2 anti-coordination settings
papers.keyFinding: Cooperative and coordinating strategies can emerge and stabilize through evolutionary pressure in anti-coordination environments, with repeated interaction enabling players to sustain equilibria that differ from one-shot Nash outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Explains how repeated social interactions shape behavior in conflict-of-interest settings such as traffic, market entry, and resource sharing, where agents prefer to differentiate rather than match

papers.title: The quasi-prekernel for cooperative games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Qianqian Kong, Hans Peters, Hao Sun
papers.rq: How can the prekernel solution concept for cooperative games be extended or relaxed to a quasi-prekernel, and what properties does this new concept satisfy?
papers.method: Axiomatic and game-theoretic analysis; formal characterization of the quasi-prekernel solution concept using properties such as excess comparisons and bilateral bargaining conditions in transferable utility cooperative games
papers.keyFinding: The quasi-prekernel is introduced as a generalization of the classical prekernel for cooperative games, retaining key desirable properties while potentially expanding existence or tractability; it satisfies a relaxed bilateral equilibrium condition that bridges the prekernel and related solution concepts
papers.whyItMatters: Refining solution concepts in cooperative game theory improves the tools available for analyzing fair division, cost sharing, and coalition formation in economics and operations research; a quasi-prekernel may be more broadly applicable or computationally accessible than the standard prekernel

papers.title: The refinement of Nash equilibrium based on equilibrium models of imperfectly rational behavior
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Rodrigo A. Velez, Alexander L. Brown
papers.rq: Can models of imperfectly rational behavior provide principled refinements of Nash equilibrium?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis linking equilibrium refinement criteria to behavioral equilibrium models such as quantal response equilibrium and logit equilibrium, examining which Nash equilibria survive as limiting cases of imperfect rationality
papers.keyFinding: Behavioral equilibrium models that incorporate imperfect rationality systematically select among Nash equilibria, offering a behaviorally grounded refinement criterion that eliminates implausible equilibria without requiring ad hoc trembles or perfection assumptions
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a unified framework connecting classical refinement theory to empirically grounded behavioral models, potentially resolving longstanding debates about equilibrium selection by anchoring refinements in observable deviations from rationality

papers.title: Timing and skewness of information revelation: Evidence on information structures and compound lotteries
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Enrico Diecidue, Thomas Langer, Sven Nolte, Sebastian Riedmiller, Judith C. Schneider
papers.rq: How do the timing and skewness of information revelation affect individual decision-making under uncertainty, specifically regarding preferences over information structures and compound lotteries?
papers.method: Controlled laboratory experiments examining choices over compound lotteries with varied information timing and skewness of revelation sequences
papers.keyFinding: Individuals exhibit systematic preferences over how and when uncertainty is resolved, with skewness of the information revelation sequence playing a significant role alongside timing, suggesting that people care not just about when they learn outcomes but about the shape of the resolution process
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals that standard models of information preferences are incomplete by ignoring skewness effects, with implications for how firms, platforms, and policymakers should design feedback and disclosure mechanisms

papers.title: Transaction fee mechanisms robust to welfare-increasing collusion
papers.abstract: Publication date: March 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 157Author(s): Yotam Gafni, Aviv Yaish
papers.rq: What transaction fee mechanisms can remain robust even when miners and users collude in welfare-increasing ways?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design and game-theoretic analysis of blockchain transaction fee mechanisms, examining collusion-proofness conditions under welfare-improving coalitions
papers.keyFinding: It is possible to design transaction fee mechanisms that are robust to welfare-increasing collusion—where miners and users coordinate to mutual benefit—without sacrificing other desirable properties, challenging the assumption that collusion-proofness and efficiency are incompatible
papers.whyItMatters: Blockchain fee markets like Ethereum's EIP-1559 are vulnerable to miner-user collusion; this work provides a formal framework for designing more robust mechanisms that preserve social welfare while resisting strategic manipulation

papers.title: Transparency and Information Acquisition in College Admissions
papers.abstract: Publication date: Available online 25 May 2026Source: Games and Economic BehaviorAuthor(s): Youngwoo Koh, Wooyoung Lim
papers.rq: Does greater transparency in college admissions criteria affect how much effort students invest in acquiring information about their own qualifications?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model analyzing strategic information acquisition by applicants under varying levels of admissions transparency
papers.keyFinding: Increased transparency in admissions criteria can reduce students' incentives to acquire costly information about their own types, potentially leading to welfare-ambiguous outcomes where transparency does not straightforwardly benefit all parties
papers.whyItMatters: Informs ongoing policy debates about college admissions reform and holistic vs. transparent criteria, revealing unintended consequences of disclosure mandates on applicant behavior and market efficiency

papers.title: Two-player binary global games without dominance solvable states
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): In-Uck Park, Efthymios Smyrniotis
papers.rq: Under what conditions do two-player binary global games lack dominance-solvable states, and what does this imply for equilibrium selection?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis of global games framework; characterization of parameter regions where iterated elimination of dominated strategies fails to yield a unique solution in two-player binary-action settings
papers.keyFinding: There exist configurations of two-player binary global games in which no dominance-solvable states exist, meaning the standard global games refinement cannot pin down a unique equilibrium through iterated dominance arguments alone
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the conventional wisdom that global games generically deliver unique equilibrium predictions via dominance solvability; has implications for coordination models in banking, currency crises, and other binary-action strategic environments

papers.title: Welfare properties of the Taiwan mechanism
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Ilan Wolff
papers.rq: What are the welfare properties of the Taiwan mechanism, a particular matching or allocation procedure?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using mechanism design and social choice frameworks to evaluate welfare outcomes of the Taiwan mechanism
papers.keyFinding: The Taiwan mechanism exhibits specific welfare properties—likely including efficiency or fairness characterizations—that distinguish it from alternative mechanisms in its class
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the welfare implications of real-world allocation mechanisms helps policymakers design or reform systems to better serve participants, particularly in education or public resource allocation contexts

papers.title: When information and communication are both costly
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shahir Safi
papers.rq: How do optimal communication strategies change when both acquiring information and communicating it are costly?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model with a sender-receiver framework incorporating dual costs for information acquisition and communication simultaneously
papers.keyFinding: When both information and communication are costly, agents strategically limit the precision and quantity of information they transmit, leading to equilibria with coarser communication than when only one cost is present; the interaction between the two costs creates non-trivial trade-offs that reduce overall information transmission relative to single-cost benchmarks
papers.whyItMatters: Most real-world communication involves both acquiring and transmitting information, yet models typically treat only one cost; understanding joint costs has implications for optimal organizational design, media markets, and regulatory disclosure policy

papers.title: When is it (im)possible to respect all individuals’ preferences under uncertainty?
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Kensei Nakamura
papers.rq: Under what conditions can a social preference ordering respect every individual's preferences when choices involve uncertainty?
papers.method: Axiomatic/theoretical analysis examining compatibility conditions between individual and social preferences under uncertainty, building on social choice and expected utility frameworks
papers.keyFinding: It is generally impossible to aggregate individual preferences under uncertainty into a coherent social preference that respects all individuals simultaneously, except under highly restrictive conditions; the paper characterizes precisely when such aggregation is and is not feasible
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies fundamental limits of welfare economics and social choice under risk, with implications for cost-benefit analysis, policy evaluation, and the design of collective decision rules when individuals have heterogeneous beliefs or risk attitudes

papers.title: A systematic overview and second-order meta-analysis of nature-based interventions for stress, anxiety and depression

papers.title: The healing power of nature reduces stress, anxiety and depression
papers.abstract: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 28 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02434-3A global analysis of more than 3,800 studies that involved over 10 million people shows that contact with nature reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression while promoting relaxation. The findings strengthen the case for integrating natural environments into mental-health strategies and urban planning policies, although rigorous trials are needed to guide practice and policy.

papers.title: Thalamic oscillations distinguish natural states of consciousness in humans
papers.abstract: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 27 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02446-zChowdhury et al. report the discovery of a 19–45-Hz thalamic oscillation that is present during human wakefulness and REM sleep, but not NREM sleep.
papers.rq: Can distinct neural oscillatory signatures in the thalamus reliably differentiate natural states of human consciousness such as wakefulness, REM sleep, and NREM sleep?
papers.method: Intracranial electrophysiological recording of thalamic activity in human subjects across natural sleep-wake cycles, identifying oscillatory frequency bands associated with each consciousness state
papers.keyFinding: A 19–45-Hz thalamic oscillation is present during wakefulness and REM sleep but absent during NREM sleep, providing a neural marker that distinguishes conscious from unconscious states
papers.whyItMatters: Identifying a reliable thalamic biomarker of consciousness has implications for diagnosing disorders of consciousness, understanding anesthesia, and advancing brain-computer interfaces; it also reinforces the thalamus as a central hub in consciousness research
